chapter: Strings, arrangements and the Shrine band
title: Robichaux arrangements, lead sheets and tricking up stock arrangements
summary: DeDroit says Dixieland bands used lead sheets rather than full parts, and describes tricking up stock arrangements with new introductions and quotations.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. Yes. Yeah. But what I was getting at on that was that a lot of those arrangements that are from his collection that he left have a lot of string parts written now, is it that he would have just discarded these and not used this part as time went on when people didn't want so many strings. Like, for instance, they have cello parts and viola parts and so forth. What kind of orchestras would have used

all those parts? Would have been in the theaters and so forth? Mr. Robichaux was a very fine musician and a very fine gentleman. And he liked me. I mean we got along great. He was the one that I borrowed the orchestration of the panel often. And I concocted my own arrangement of it, you see. And you'd just have to take the parts. The truth of the matter is, in the Dixieland we didn't write parts. We wrote a lead sheet. Which is? With the chords for the piano playing. I'd have to find me doing better than you, you see. And then we'd run over the tune, and maybe we wouldn't. But everybody knew Panama. From hearing it, I don't know where. So Parenti would make his chorus and it would be great, and Barry would play his and it would be great. I'd play one, the other player might take one, and we'd play another song. Or we might play up until the 24th ball and we'd come in on the last eight balls, you know, and sock it out. But the violins went out of mine. They didn't go out, but they weren't used much for dance music. Dixieland and our noisy music was taken over, you see.

So you used to alter the, well, you talked in one, in your other interview about sometimes some new tune came out, you'd get the stock arrangement and then you'd have a few iterations on it and then you'd

have your own. Well I'll tell you what, the stocks used to come out so fast that I couldn't make arrangements on everything, you see. So I would trick it, what I call it trick it, trick it up. And it got so that when the other band leaders would come on the boat, just to hear what I was doing, they'd say, playing all specials. I'd say yes. That was the stock. I'd let the saxophone play, get them to play eight bars of Blue Moon, you know, and then when the other guys come in, it sounds like quite loud, it sounds like a big band, you know. Or I might start changing the introduction. Some introductions some bands couldn't play. I'll give you one. One example, there's an arrangement called the Sugar Bowl Medley now that consists of Way Down Yonder in New Orleans and The Saints. It's published. And the introduction goes, half the saxophone players can't get the notes out. If it was left to me I could give them two half notes on the bar so they could be swinging when they got into the thing. Well we used it in the Shrine Band. I said, let's cut it out. You fellas can't play it. They don't like to hear that, you see. I was the leader of the Shrine Band for 1971 and 72. And I had wonderful plans for them, but they didn't go along with me. They preferred to have a good time with me. Rather than sectional rehearsals. They didn't want sectional rehearsals because you'd find out who was making the bad news. They couldn't fool me. I could tell them from where I was standing. You know? But they're all men and means and they're just not getting paid and they pick up their own walk right now. And they had 35 men one night, nine the next. Sometimes they'd be playing, I'd stop directing and be playing. I'm reached in but they're playing. I can't stand it. I can't go with that kind of stuff.
